flashcards.q: What are the two computational primitives every RAGAS/DeepEval metric reduces to?
flashcards.a: (a) Claim decomposition + judge verdict (faithfulness, context recall, hallucination) and (b) reverse-question generation + embedding similarity (answer relevancy).

flashcards.q: Roughly how many LLM calls does computing faithfulness cost for one example?
flashcards.a: 1 call to decompose the answer into atomic claims (typically 3-6 claims) plus 1 call per claim to check support = about 4-7 calls total.

flashcards.q: What is faithfulness blind to, by construction?
flashcards.a: Whether the retrieved context itself is correct. A faithful answer grounded in a wrong retrieved chunk still scores 1.0 because faithfulness only checks the answer against context, never against the world.

flashcards.q: What is answer relevancy blind to, by construction?
flashcards.a: Factual correctness. It only measures topical alignment via reverse-generated questions and embedding similarity, so a confidently wrong but on-topic answer scores well.

flashcards.q: Roughly what judge rerun flip rate has been measured on LLM-judge pairwise comparisons under identical conditions?
flashcards.a: About 14% mean flip rate (2026 study, 'The Coin Flip Judge?'), meaning roughly 1 in 7 pairwise verdicts changes on an identical re-run.

flashcards.q: Roughly how many paired examples are needed to reliably detect a 5-point mean shift in a continuous eval score like faithfulness?
flashcards.a: About 100-250 paired examples (using sigma~0.15-0.25, delta=0.05, 80% power, alpha=0.05) with a paired difference test, not a raw before/after comparison of means.

flashcards.q: Why must you use a paired test rather than comparing two independent means when checking an eval score delta?
flashcards.a: Because the same examples are run before and after the change, so per-example score differences are correlated; a paired test on those differences has more power to detect a real shift than comparing two unpaired sample means.

flashcards.q: What does DeepEval's assert_test() actually do?
flashcards.a: Runs specified metrics against an LLMTestCase, gets back continuous 0-1 scores and reasons, and raises a pytest assertion failure if any score is below its configured threshold -- a normal assertion wrapped around a noisy LLM-judge output.

flashcards.q: What is DeepEval's GEval metric, mechanically?
flashcards.a: A reusable metric class implementing the G-Eval technique: given a plain-English criterion, it generates its own chain-of-thought evaluation steps and scores against them rather than using a fixed metric definition.

flashcards.q: What are Promptfoo's three assertion tiers, cheapest first?
flashcards.a: Deterministic (contains, equals, regex, cost, latency -- free and instant), model-graded (llm-rubric, similar, answer-relevance -- sends output to a judge LLM), and custom code (inline JavaScript/Python).

flashcards.q: What specific gap does Promptfoo fill that a full RAGAS/DeepEval harness doesn't?
flashcards.a: Fast, CI-native prompt-level regression testing across a matrix of providers/models for a specific prompt change, without needing to stand up a full retrieval/generation attribution harness.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between LangSmith's offline evaluate() and its online evaluators?
flashcards.a: evaluate()/aevaluate() runs a system against a versioned dataset producing a comparable experiment. Online evaluators score live production traces continuously and reference-free, feeding the same dashboards without a pre-built dataset.

flashcards.q: What can LangSmith show that RAGAS, DeepEval, and Promptfoo alone cannot?
flashcards.a: A regression in eval score joined to the cost and latency of the exact trace that produced it, since traces, evals, and cost all live in one system.

flashcards.q: Why is upgrading RAGAS/DeepEval/LangSmith to a new version a calibration risk, not just a version bump?
flashcards.a: These frameworks' built-in metric prompts and sometimes their default judge models can change silently between minor versions with no changelog entry most teams read, shifting the score distribution exactly like an unannounced judge-model swap.

flashcards.q: Why is running RAGAS, DeepEval, and LangSmith evals all in parallel 'for redundancy' a bad plan?
flashcards.a: All three implement close variants of the same claim-decomposition primitive, so you roughly triple judge-call cost for correlated noise rather than three independent measurements.
